# Motivation {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## The Biomarker Data Gap

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
- Micronutrient deficiency drives child and maternal morbidity across sub-Saharan Africa,
  yet nationally representative **biochemical surveys are rare**
- Blood-based biomarker collection (retinol, ferritin, zinc) requires cold-chain logistics
  and laboratory capacity; surveys occur at **decadal intervals**
- National micronutrient surveys (e.g., Gambia GMS, Ghana DHS+, Sierra Leone MNS, Malawi MNS)
  are among the few nationally representative individual-level biomarker datasets in the region
- Between survey cycles, **sub-national burden is essentially unknown**; program allocation
  relies on outdated or modelled estimates
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
*Suggested: schematic survey-gap timeline*
*(no figure file available)*
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Frame the problem narrowly: we are not trying to replace surveys. We are extracting maximum information from nationally representative biomarker surveys across four countries by leveraging correlated proxy data to produce sub-national estimates.
:::

---

## Policy Need and Current Modeling Gaps

**Sub-national estimates are required for:**

- Targeted supplementation and food fortification allocation
- Resource prioritization under SUN and GAIN frameworks
- Baseline characterization for cluster-randomized trials

**Limitations of existing approaches:**

| Approach | Key limitation |
|---|---|
| Geostatistical / GP models | Requires spatially dense observations; no high-dimensional predictors |
| Small-area estimation | Strong distributional assumptions; requires auxiliary frame overlap |
| Survey weighting | Cannot extrapolate beyond sampled locations; no out-of-sample uncertainty |

> **Our approach:** Data-adaptive ensemble trained on survey data; predict at individual level using nationally available proxy predictors; aggregate to Admin1.

::: {.notes}
Survey clusters do not span all Admin1 units uniformly in any country. Prediction fills spatial gaps using predictor similarity to observed clusters, not spatial smoothing.
:::

---

## Objective

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Primary objective:** Estimate Admin1 and national prevalence of vitamin A deficiency
(VAD) and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) for children and women across four countries
(Gambia, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Malawi) using a SuperLearner ensemble with multi-source
proxy predictors.
:::

**Secondary objectives:**

- Quantify Admin1 and national prediction uncertainty via cluster-level bootstrap (95% CI)
- Assess domain-specific contribution to predictive performance via permutation-based domain ablation
- Evaluate cross-country transportability via leave-one-country-out (LOCO) validation
- Identify key predictor themes via conceptual variable importance analysis

---

# Data Architecture {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Outcome and Population Structure

**Data sources:** Individual-level biochemical surveys with cluster GPS coordinates from four countries:
Gambia (GMS), Ghana (DHS+), Sierra Leone (MNS), Malawi (MNS).
Each country contributes ~2,000-5,000 individuals; ~2,500 merged proxy predictor columns per country after leakage exclusion.

**Four outcomes, fitted independently per country:**

| Population | Micronutrient | Continuous marker | Binary threshold | Adjustment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Children | Vitamin A | RBP (µmol/L) | < 0.70 µmol/L → VAD | Thurnham |
| Women | Vitamin A | RBP (µmol/L) | < 0.70 µmol/L → VAD | Thurnham |
| Children | Iron | log(Ferritin µg/L) | ferritin < 12 µg/L → IDA | Brinda |
| Women | Iron | log(Ferritin µg/L) | ferritin < 15 µg/L → IDA | Brinda |

- Population split by country-specific child flag (e.g., `gw_child_flag`); non-overlapping subsets
- Cluster identifier per country (e.g., `gw_cnum`) — used for blocked CV folds and bootstrap resampling

**Sample sizes vary by country** — see results report for current per-country totals.

::: {.notes}
Both a continuous SL (squared error loss) and binary SL (logistic loss) are fit for each outcome. Binary model predictions are used for prevalence estimation when available; continuous model is retained for RMSE evaluation and as fallback.
:::

---

## Predictor Strategy: Proxy-Only Models

**Primary analysis uses proxy predictors only** — external data sources available
without a concurrent biomarker survey. Country-specific survey domains (e.g., `gw_`)
are **excluded** because they contain biomarkers, nutrition indicators, and anthropometry
from the same survey as the outcome, producing artificially inflated AUC (near 1.0).

| Domain | Prefix | Source | Approx. N cols | In primary model |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DHS | `dhs_` | DHS cluster-level aggregates | 1,875 | Yes |
| MICS | `mics_` | MICS cluster-level aggregates | 290 | Yes |
| IHME | `ihme_` | IHME geospatial estimates | 60 | Yes |
| MAP | `MAP_` | Malaria Atlas Project rasters | 26 | Yes |
| WFP | `wfp_` | WFP market access / food security | 46 | Yes |
| GEE | `gee_` | Google Earth Engine satellite covariates | 142 | Yes |
| **FSEC** | `fsec_` | HFID + Cadre Harmonise food security | varies | Yes |
| LSMS | `lsms_` | LSMS household consumption | **0** | -- (absent) |
| ~~Survey~~ | ~~`gw_`/`gh_`/etc.~~ | ~~Country survey covariates~~ | ~~varies~~ | **No** (leakage) |
| **Total proxy** | | | **~2,500** | **~2,500** |

**Why exclude survey domains?** Country-specific survey columns include raw biomarkers,
inflammation markers, anemia indicators, and anthropometry -- all measured in the same
survey as the outcome. Including them inflates AUC to ~1.0 but does not reflect
real-world prediction accuracy.

::: {.notes}
The proxy-only approach answers the operationally relevant question: "how well can we predict micronutrient deficiency from routinely available data?" Expected AUC is 0.60-0.80, which is modest but useful for screening and prioritization. The survey-inclusive model serves as a supplementary upper-bound analysis. The new FSEC domain integrates food insecurity data from HFID and Cadre Harmonise datasets.
:::

---

# Modeling Strategy {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## SuperLearner Ensemble: Learner Library

**FAST stack** — 3 base learners, NNLS metalearner, binomial log-likelihood loss

| # | Learner | Algorithm | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `lrnr_mean` | Intercept / mean | Baseline |
| 2 | `lrnr_lasso` | Lasso (glmnet, alpha = 1) | L1-penalized GLM |
| 3 | `ranger_lrnr` | Random forest (`ranger`, min.node.size = 10) | Conservative trees |

**FULL stack** — 7 base learners (used for publication runs)

| # | Learner | Algorithm | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `lrnr_mean` | Intercept / mean | Baseline |
| 2 | `lrnr_lasso` | Lasso (alpha = 1) | L1 penalty |
| 3 | `lrnr_enet` | Elastic net (alpha = 0.75) | Mixed L1/L2 |
| 4 | `lrnr_ridge` | Ridge (alpha = 0) | L2 penalty |
| 5 | `ranger_conservative` | Random forest (conservative) | Larger min.node.size |
| 6 | `ranger_deeper` | Random forest (deeper) | Smaller min.node.size |
| 7 | `xgboost_lrnr` | XGBoost | Gradient boosting |

- **Metalearner:** NNLS (`Lrnr_nnls`) — non-negative, sum-to-one; interpretable convex combination
- **Continuous fallback**: identical stack with squared error loss
- **No screener pipelines** — removed because they crashed with p >> n in multi-country data
- **NNLS learner weights:** See results report for current per-country weight allocations

::: {.notes}
The previous pipeline used prescreened learners (cor_glm, rf_prescreened) to reduce dimensionality, but these crashed with p >> n in multi-country datasets. The current stacks rely on regularization (lasso/ridge/elastic net) and tree-based learners that handle high-dimensional data natively.
:::

---

## Preprocessing Pipeline and Cross-Validation Design

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Preprocessing** (inside `DHS_SL_clustered`, `src/analysis/sl_helpers.R`):

1. Drop all-NA columns
2. Near-zero variance removal (`caret::nearZeroVar`)
3. Missing value imputation — median/mode + binary missingness indicators (`ck37r`)
4. Second NZV pass (post-imputation indicators may be near-zero)
5. Marginal association prescreen: `washb_prescreen(pval = 0.20)` — retains predictors with p < 0.20 marginal association
6. `recipes` pipeline: `step_zv` → `step_nzv` → `step_corr(r > 0.85)` → `step_normalize`
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Cross-validation design:**

- K = **5** folds
- **Cluster-blocked:** `origami::make_folds(cluster_ids = cluster_id, V = 5)`
- No cluster contributes to both training and validation in any fold
- Prevents within-cluster correlation from inflating CV performance
- Rationale: Survey clusters contain O(10-25) individuals with correlated outcomes; standard random split would inflate AUC
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Cluster-blocking is the single most important design choice for CV validity in survey data. Standard random individual splitting in clustered data produces optimistic AUC estimates because the learner sees correlated individuals from the same cluster in both the training and validation fold. This applies identically across all four countries.
:::

---

## Bootstrap Uncertainty: Cluster-Level Resampling

**Bootstrap run for one illustrative country x outcome** (Malawi women_vitA, B = 100 in fast mode) to save compute. Full-mode: B >= 200 per country x outcome for publication.

**Algorithm per replicate:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Sample *N*~clusters~ clusters **with replacement** (not individuals) |
| 2 | Reconstruct individual-level dataset from resampled clusters |
| 3 | **Refit** full SL ensemble on bootstrap sample (including all preprocessing) |
| 4 | **Predict** on all individuals in the **original** dataset |
| 5 | Aggregate to Admin1 mean prevalence and national mean prevalence |

**Outputs:** Mean, 2.5th, 97.5th percentiles across B replicates → 95% percentile CI

**CIs capture:** finite-sample variability + ensemble weight variability + prescreening variability
**CIs do not capture:** model misspecification, distribution shift, extrapolation uncertainty

::: {.notes}
Current illustrative bootstrap uses Malawi women_vitA with B=100. Prediction on the original full dataset (step 4) rather than the bootstrap-resampled dataset stabilises Admin1 aggregation. The bootstrap refit is computationally expensive because the full preprocessing + SL stack runs B times per country x outcome.
:::

# Within-Country Performance {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## CV Performance: Continuous Models

> Source: `results/tables/cv_performance_all.csv` — results for all four countries
> See results report for full per-country tables

CV performance varies by country and outcome. See the results report for current values across Gambia, Ghana, Sierra Leone, and Malawi.

- RMSE is on the biomarker scale (µmol/L for RBP; log µg/L for ferritin) — do not compare across micronutrients
- AUC computed by treating the continuous prediction as a ranking score for the binary threshold
- R² reported relative to null model (intercept only); can be negative if SL performs worse than the mean

::: {.notes}
R² can be negative if the SL performs worse than the mean. R² vs. mean (R2_vs_mean column) is a more stable reference. AUC for the continuous model serves as a comparison baseline for the binary model AUC. Performance varies substantially across countries due to differing predictor coverage and sample sizes.
:::

---

## CV Performance: Binary Models

> Source: `results/tables/cv_performance_all.csv` — results for all four countries
> See results report for full per-country tables

Binary model AUC, Brier scores, and calibration statistics are computed per country x outcome. See the results report for current values across all four countries.

*Null Brier = prev x (1 - prev); compute from observed prevalence.*

- **Perfect calibration:** intercept = 0, slope = 1
- Slope < 1 -> predicted probabilities are too extreme (over-dispersion)
- Slope > 1 -> predicted probabilities are too conservative
- Binary model preferred for prevalence estimation when its AUC >= continuous model AUC

::: {.notes}
Calibration regression: logit(predicted probability) ~ observed binary outcome. The Brier score is prevalence-sensitive; always compare to null model Brier to assess whether the model adds value. Cross-country variation in AUC reflects differences in predictor informativeness and outcome prevalence.
:::

---

## Admin1 Observed vs. Predicted Prevalence

Admin1 scatter plots are generated per country x outcome. See the results report for current figures across all four countries.

*Dashed line = 45-degree identity. Points above = over-prediction; below = under-prediction.*

- Each country has a different number of Admin1 units (Gambia: 5-8; Ghana: 10; Sierra Leone: 14; Malawi: 28)
- R-squared on a small N of Admin1 units is unstable; interpret alongside individual-level AUC
- Systematic deviation from the identity line indicates a national-scale calibration issue

::: {.notes}
Admin1 scatter plots are produced by the targets pipeline for each country x outcome combination. Countries with more Admin1 units (e.g., Malawi with 28 districts) provide more stable area-level validation.
:::

---

## Evaluating Models for Rare Outcomes

**Three dimensions of model quality:**

| Dimension | Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Discrimination** | ROC-AUC, **PR-AUC** | Can the model rank individuals by risk? |
| **Calibration** | Cal. slope, Cal. intercept | Are predicted probabilities accurate? |
| **Prevalence recovery** | Predicted vs. observed prevalence | Does the model get the right burden estimate? |

**Why standard AUC can mislead:**

- With 5% prevalence, predicting "not deficient" for everyone gives 95% accuracy
- PR-AUC is more informative: a no-skill classifier has PR-AUC = prevalence
- For **subnational mapping**, calibration and prevalence recovery matter more than discrimination

::: {.notes}
The goal of this project is area-level prevalence estimation, not individual diagnosis. A model with AUC = 0.60 can still recover area-level prevalence well if it is properly calibrated. The key question is: does the model systematically over- or under-estimate prevalence in different areas? Calibration slope near 1 and intercept near 0 indicate good aggregate performance even when individual-level discrimination is modest.
:::

# Subnational Results {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Admin1 Predicted Deficiency Prevalence

Admin1 predicted vs. observed prevalence tables are generated per country. See the results report for full tables across Gambia, Ghana, Sierra Leone, and Malawi.

- Predicted prevalence = mean binary SL predicted probability per Admin1 unit
- Observed prevalence = mean of pre-computed Thurnham/Brinda-adjusted binary indicator
- Interpretation: Admin1 units with largest obs-pred discrepancy warrant qualitative review of local predictor values
- Admin1 error tables available in `results/tables/admin2_error_all.csv`

::: {.notes}
For Admin1 units with thin survey cluster coverage, predictions are genuine extrapolations based on predictor similarity to well-sampled units. The scatter plots (previous slide) visualise this obs-pred agreement directly. Multi-country comparison reveals which countries have the best-calibrated Admin1 predictions.
:::

---

## National Prevalence with 95% Confidence Intervals

Bootstrap CIs are currently available for the illustrative case: **Malawi women_vitA (B = 100, fast mode)**. See the results report for current bootstrap CI values.

- National estimate = mean predicted probability across all individuals with non-missing Admin1
- 95% CI = 2.5th / 97.5th percentile of B bootstrap replicates
- **Coherence check:** predicted mean should be close to observed survey prevalence (< 5 pp divergence expected); large divergence indicates calibration drift at national scale
- Full-mode bootstrap (B >= 200 per country x outcome) is needed for publication-grade CIs

::: {.notes}
Current results use B=100 for one illustrative country x outcome (Malawi women_vitA). Full-mode runs with B=200-500 per country x outcome are needed for stable intervals across all countries. For publication-grade CIs on tail percentiles, use B=500-1000.
:::

---

# Uncertainty and Robustness {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Bootstrap CI Width by Admin1

**CI width = `ci_hi - ci_lo` per Admin1 unit across B replicates.**

Bootstrap CI widths are available for the illustrative case (Malawi women_vitA, B = 100). See the results report for current values.

- CI width expected to be inversely related to number of survey clusters per Admin1
- **Interpretation:** Wide CIs do not indicate model failure — they indicate genuine statistical uncertainty given the survey design
- **Practical implication:** Admin1 units with widest CIs are where additional biomarker data collection has highest marginal value for reducing uncertainty

::: {.notes}
Bootstrap CIs propagate sampling uncertainty (cluster resampling) plus model uncertainty (refitting the ensemble per replicate, including data-adaptive prescreening, which produces different feature sets per replicate). They do not propagate misspecification or extrapolation uncertainty.
:::

---

## What the CIs Do and Do Not Cover

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Captured by cluster bootstrap:**

- Finite-sample variability in cluster composition
- Variability in ensemble NNLS weights across resamples
- Prescreening variability (data-adaptive feature selection differs per replicate)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Not captured:**

- Model misspecification (wrong functional form, omitted predictors)
- Predictor domain measurement error (satellite co-registration, survey vintage)
- Distribution shift: biomarker–predictor relationship varies across Admin1 units
- Extrapolation uncertainty for Admin1 units with no nearby survey clusters
:::
::::

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
These are **uncertainty intervals conditional on the model class and predictor set** —
not posterior predictive intervals over all possible model specifications.
:::

---

# Domain Ablation Results {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Domain Contribution: Permutation-Based Ablation

**Method: Permutation-based domain ablation** — for each domain, shuffle all its columns
(breaking the association with the outcome) and re-evaluate the trained model. No model
refitting is required, making this computationally efficient across 4 countries x 4 outcomes.

**ΔAUC = AUC(full model) - AUC(model with domain shuffled)**
Positive -> domain contributes to discrimination; negative -> domain adds noise.

Results are computed per country x outcome. See `results/tables/domain_ablation_all.csv` and the results report for full tables.

**Two types of domain ablation are now available:**

1. **Data-source ablation** — shuffles domains by data source prefix (DHS, MICS, IHME, MAP, WFP, GEE, FSEC)
2. **Conceptual ablation** — shuffles domains by thematic category (Climate, Food Security, Child Health, Fertility, Malaria, etc.) using DHS indicator lookup to classify ~2,500 predictors

::: {.notes}
Ablation is a marginal permutation-based method, not causal. Two correlated domains may each show low individual delta-AUC even though jointly they contribute substantially. The conceptual ablation provides a complementary view by grouping predictors by topic rather than data source, revealing which thematic areas drive prediction.
:::

---

## Policy Implications of Domain Contributions

**Interpretation depends on which domain dominates:**

| Dominant domain | Interpretation | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **GW** (survey covariates) | Model relies on survey-specific socioeconomic data | No new survey → no reliable prediction |
| **GEE / MAP** (remote sensing) | Spatial signal drives prediction | Satellite-based estimation feasible; gridded prediction viable |
| **DHS / MICS** (survey aggregates) | Estimates depend on external survey vintage | Outdated DHS data may degrade predictions post-survey year |
| **WFP / LSMS** (food security) | Market access and poverty are key drivers | Intervention should target food-insecure areas |

**Conceptual variable importance:**

- ~2,500 proxy predictors classified into DHS-derived categories (Child Health, Fertility, Malaria, Climate, Food Security, etc.) using official DHS indicator lookup
- Reveals which thematic areas drive prediction, complementing data-source ablation
- See `results/conceptual_ablation/` for per-country results

---

# Transportability {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Leave-One-Country-Out (LOCO) Cross-Validation

**Design:** Train the SuperLearner on 3 countries, predict on the held-out 4th country.
Repeat for each of the 4 countries as the held-out set.

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Select one country as the held-out test set |
| 2 | Train the full SL pipeline on the remaining 3 countries |
| 3 | Predict on all individuals in the held-out country |
| 4 | Evaluate AUC, Brier score, and Admin1 prevalence recovery |

**Key findings:** See `results/tables/transportability_loco_results.csv` and the results report for current LOCO AUC values across all country x outcome combinations.

- LOCO AUC is generally lower than within-country CV AUC, reflecting cross-country heterogeneity in the biomarker-predictor relationship
- Some country x outcome combinations transport better than others
- Countries with more similar predictor distributions show better transportability

::: {.notes}
LOCO validation is the strongest test of model generalizability. Performance degradation from within-country CV to LOCO indicates the degree to which country-specific patterns drive prediction. This analysis was not available in the original Gambia-only pipeline.
:::

---

# Methodological Reflections {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

---

## Strengths

1. **No post-hoc threshold tuning** — Binary SL directly maximizes log-likelihood for the binary deficiency outcome; clinical thresholds (Thurnham/Brinda) are pre-specified independently of the predictor data

2. **Cluster-blocked cross-validation** — No cluster contributes to both training and validation in any fold; reported AUC and RMSE are honest out-of-sample estimates at the individual level

3. **Explicit uncertainty quantification** — Bootstrap CIs propagate both sampling and model uncertainty; outputs include intervals, not only point estimates

4. **Reproducible, configurable pipeline** — All parameters centralised in `config.R` (K, B, thresholds, domain prefixes, leakage patterns); currently running across four countries with standardised outputs

5. **Data-adaptive ensemble** — NNLS weights respond to empirical performance of each base learner per outcome; no learner is hard-coded as dominant

6. **Cross-country transportability** — LOCO validation provides honest out-of-country prediction assessment, beyond within-country CV

::: {.notes}
The pipeline separation (sl_helpers.R defining DHS_SL_clustered and one_bootstrap, sourced independently of model fitting) means function updates do not require re-running expensive model fits.
:::

---

## Limitations

1. **Survey support dependence** — Admin1 units with no nearby survey clusters are extrapolated purely from predictor similarity; a stronger assumption than interpolation within the survey support

2. **No spatial random effects** — Individuals treated as conditionally independent given predictors; spatial autocorrelation in residuals is not modelled (a Gaussian process component would be more principled for gridded prediction)

3. **Static predictor vintage** — External domain data (DHS, MICS, IHME) reflects a fixed survey year; predictive performance may degrade as these data become stale relative to the target year

4. **Bootstrap coverage limited** — Full bootstrap (B >= 200) currently run only for one illustrative country x outcome (Malawi women_vitA); remaining country x outcome combinations need full-mode runs for publication-grade CIs

5. **Cross-country heterogeneity** — NNLS weights and predictor importance vary across countries; LOCO transportability analysis shows performance degradation when predicting on held-out countries, indicating the biomarker-predictor relationship is not fully portable

## Summary

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**One-paragraph summary**

This pipeline applies a SuperLearner ensemble (sl3, R) to estimate Admin1 and national
prevalence of vitamin A deficiency (VAD) and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) for children
and women across four countries (Gambia, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Malawi), using individual-level
biomarker survey data as the outcome and multi-source proxy predictor domains -- household
survey aggregates (DHS, MICS), geospatial covariates (GEE, MAP), food security indicators
(WFP, FSEC), and health estimates (IHME) -- as features. The ensemble integrates base learners
(lasso, elastic net, ridge, random forest, xgboost) under non-negative least squares
meta-learning with cluster-blocked 5-fold cross-validation. Binary deficiency models directly
optimize log-likelihood loss, avoiding post-hoc threshold instability. Permutation-based domain
ablation and conceptual variable importance identify the relative contribution of each predictor
domain and thematic area. Leave-one-country-out (LOCO) cross-validation evaluates
transportability across countries. Cluster-level bootstrap propagates sampling and model
uncertainty into 95% CIs for Admin1 and national prevalence.
:::
